title: Read before you edit
content: Before changing code, read the task and the code it touches, and list every place the change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports.
evidence: Source: ponytail skill, section 'Before you write'.

title: Smallest complete change
content: Solve the whole task with the least new code. No abstraction, option, config or 'for later' code nobody asked for. Still finish every part the task needs, including the callers and tests the change breaks.
evidence: Source: ponytail skill, section 'The smallest complete change'.

title: Reuse before writing
content: Take the first option that fully works: what already exists in this codebase, then the standard library or platform, then an installed dependency. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
evidence: Source: ponytail skill, ordered list of 'The smallest complete change'.

title: Fix the root cause once
content: For a bug fix, grep every caller of the function you touch before editing, then fix the cause in the shared code instead of patching one call site.

title: Never cut safety to stay small
content: Keep validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security checks and accessibility. Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
evidence: Source: ponytail skill, 'Never cut' and the rule on moved code.

title: New logic leaves a check
content: Non-trivial new logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security code) leaves one small test or assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
evidence: Source: ponytail skill, rule 'Lazy code without its check is unfinished'.

title: Run it before you say it works
content: Do not report a change as working until you ran the test or command that proves it, and read its output. A claim without a run is a guess.
evidence: Claake Code plan, lots C2/C4: run guards are judged on disk because the model's own claim of success was not reliable; test 'guard_refuses_end_of_turn_until_file_exists'.

title: Say what you did not test
content: End a report with what you skipped or did not check and any risk the user must know. Keep 'tested' and 'not tested' clearly apart.
evidence: Source: ponytail skill, opening paragraph (closing lines of every reply).

title: Check which build you are testing
content: Before a manual test, confirm that the running program is the build that contains your change (process path, version, start time). An installed app and a dev build can run side by side.
evidence: Claake Code, lot D1: three manual checks of the learning switch were made in the installed app, which did not contain the change; the database showed the switch had never been written.

title: Guard scripted edits
content: When you edit a file with a script or a pattern, assert that the pattern matches exactly once before replacing, then read the result. A loose pattern edits the wrong place silently.
evidence: Claake Code, lot C5: a regex inserted 'verify_command: None' into the wrong struct of remote.rs; the compiler caught it (E0573).

title: Stage only your own files
content: Commit with explicit paths. Never use 'git add -A' in a repository that has changes you did not make, and never revert or delete files you did not create.
evidence: Claake Code plan, REGLES.md: the user's unrelated files (videos, .blend, images) stayed out of every commit by staging explicit paths.

title: Bound every wait
content: Give every command, test and loop a timeout or a retry limit. When a test hangs, stop it and find why; do not wait longer.
evidence: Claake Code, lot C4: the first scripted-loop tests hung for minutes because a closed command channel made the loop spin; fixed in test_support.rs.

title: Short replies, exact terms
content: Drop filler, pleasantries and hedging. Keep technical terms, code, commands and error strings exact and verbatim. Quote the shortest decisive error line, not the whole log.

title: Full sentences when it is risky
content: For security warnings, irreversible actions and multi-step sequences where order matters, write complete, unambiguous sentences; go back to short replies afterwards.
